summary: This document is a screenshot of a ResearchGate discussion thread posted by Garrick Holmes (affiliated with Rifor) on November 25, 2026, presenting a preprint titled "Water as an Electrical Structure: Hydrogen Bond Asymmetry in the DNA Hydration Shell and Flexoelectric Charging of Ice." The preprint advances two hypotheses: (1) that hydrogen bond asymmetry in water's hydration shell around DNA's minor groove forms part of DNA's electrical pathway, and (2) that flexoelectric mechanisms in ice drive electrification leading to lightning. A peer review by Yuri Mirgorod is included, noting the work is at the hypothesis-generation stage with proposed but not yet executed experiments.

content_blocks.title: Discussion Post: Water as an Electrical Structure (Preprint Overview)
content_blocks.content: Garrick Holmes (Rifor) posted a ResearchGate discussion titled 'Water as an Electrical Structure: Hydrogen Bond Asymmetry in the DNA Hydration Shell and Flexoelectric Charging of Ice.' The abstract states: 'Water does more than fill the space around living things and storms. Its hydrogen bonds hold electric charge and steer where it goes, and this paper follows that one idea into two places no one has connected. Inside DNA, ordered water in the groove...' Tags: Fees and Charges, Ice, Hydrogen Bonding, Lightning, Hydration. Attachments include a JPEG figure (295 kB) and the full document (353 kB).

content_blocks.title: Peer Review by Yuri Mirgorod – Summary of Preprint
content_blocks.content: Yuri Mirgorod provided a review of the preprint. Summary: The work advances two hypotheses resting on a single idea — the hydrogen bond of water is an electrical structure, and the arrangement of water's hydrogen bonds determines how charge is held and where it goes. Part I connects the donor-bond asymmetry of the water molecule (Gunkel et al., 2024) with the ordered hydration shell of the minor groove of DNA and proposes that this shell forms part of DNA's electrical pathway. Part II develops the flexoelectric mechanism of ice electrification into quantitative estimates: time to the first lightning flash (8–28 minutes), a laboratory test using a bilayer of amorphous ice with a built-in control, and a predicted tidal electrical signal from ice shelves.

content_blocks.title: Peer Review – Strengths
content_blocks.content: Strengths identified by Mirgorod: (1) The method of 'field synthesis' is declared honestly — the author explicitly separates the measured from the conjectured (Section XVI), and every figure can be checked with a calculator. This is described as a rare discipline for interdisciplinary work. (2) The proposed experiments are feasible with existing methods, and three of the four in Part I contain a built-in null hypothesis (the mass isotope effect as an alternative to the asymmetry mechanism). (3) The numerical estimate of the time to the first flash (Tables 1–2) is a strong point: it converts a qualitative idea into a testable range consistent with radar observations.

content_blocks.title: Peer Review – Comments and Questions (Weaknesses/Gaps)
content_blocks.content: Critical comments from Mirgorod: (1) The donor-bond asymmetry (Gunkel et al.) was measured on dilute water in dimethylformamide — the paper should explicitly discuss whether the effect transfers to pure water and to nanometer-scale confinement. (2) The estimate of charge per collision (0.16–1.5 fC) rests on an assumed strain of ~1%; sensitivity to this parameter should be shown explicitly. (3) The hypothesis that the hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway competes with the conventional interpretation of charge transport along the stack of bases (Slinker et al.); Section VI D should specify how to distinguish the shell's contribution from the bases' contribution within a single measurement. (4) Part II is stronger than Part I in terms of self-containment: the 'bend — polarization — charge stripping by the quasi-liquid skin' mechanics is written out step by step and includes a decisive control (the symmetric sandwich). Part I lacks an equivalent 'killer' experiment.

content_blocks.title: Peer Review – Comparison with Quantum-Thermal Transitions (QTT)
content_blocks.content: Mirgorod notes that while the preprint does not use the term 'quantum-thermal transitions (QTT)', several blocks lie in the same conceptual plane: (i) the critical point between low-density and high-density liquid water at ~210 K (Section IX); (ii) nuclear quantum effects in the hydrogen bond (Flór et al.); (iii) the hopping proton transfer along chains of hydrogen bonds (Grotthuss mechanism). The divergence: transitions in the preprint are thermal and mechanical, with no electrochemical component and no entropy–enthalpy analysis. The H₂O/D₂O substitution test proposed by the author also works as a discriminator of the quantum-nuclear nature of the effect.

content_blocks.title: Peer Review – Recommendation
content_blocks.content: Mirgorod's recommendation: 'The work is valuable as a generator of testable hypotheses rather than as an established result, and the author says so explicitly. Publication in its current form — with caution; after revisions addressing points 1–4 — as a preprint aimed at attracting experimentalists to the proposed tests, above all the amorphous-ice bilayer and isotope substitution.' This confirms the work is at an early, hypothesis-generation stage (TRL 1–2), with no completed experiments reported.

content_blocks.title: Reply by Amin Shamsabadipour
content_blocks.content: Amin Shamsabadipour added a reply 3 hours after the post, attaching a document titled 'Charge (Unit Convention, Quantum Realization, and Symmetry).pdf' (1.54 MB), described as a 'full document, which can be usefully applicable.' No further scientific content is visible from this reply.

key_findings: The preprint is at TRL 1–2: it advances two theoretical hypotheses with quantitative estimates but no completed experiments.
Part I hypothesis: hydrogen bond donor asymmetry in water (Gunkel et al., 2024) creates an ordered hydration shell in DNA's minor groove that forms part of DNA's electrical pathway.

Part II hypothesis: flexoelectric mechanism in ice drives charge separation leading to lightning; quantitative estimate of time to first lightning flash is 8–28 minutes, consistent with radar observations.
Estimated charge per ice collision: 0.16–1.5 fC, based on an assumed strain of ~1% (sensitivity not fully characterized).
Proposed experiments include: amorphous ice bilayer with symmetric sandwich control, H₂O/D₂O isotope substitution test, and experiments with built-in null hypotheses (mass isotope effect).
Key weakness: donor-bond asymmetry data (Gunkel et al.) was measured in dilute water in dimethylformamide, not in pure water or nanometer-scale confinement relevant to DNA.
Competing hypothesis for DNA charge transport: conventional base-stacking pathway (Slinker et al.) not yet distinguished from the hydration shell pathway.
Peer reviewer (Mirgorod) recommends publication as a preprint to attract experimentalists; no experimental validation has been performed.
The author explicitly separates measured from conjectured content (Section XVI), indicating intellectual honesty but also confirming the speculative nature of the work.
A predicted tidal electrical signal from ice shelves is included as a testable prediction of the flexoelectric model.
